text: Course 4 covered the Flow Execution Log in detail — the execution record for each run of a flow, and the run history that lets you open any past execution and see what each step did, including the resolved values a data pill actually held. That lesson taught you to read the log. This lesson is about what you're reading it for when a flow in production is reported as a problem.

When a stakeholder says a flow is stuck, they mean one thing: nothing visible has happened for a while, and they're worried. But that idle state can mean two very different things, and they demand opposite responses.

A flow can be genuinely failed — an actual error occurred at a step, and execution stopped there until someone intervenes. Or it can be correctly paused, most often sitting at an Approval step, legitimately waiting for someone to action a request that simply hasn't been touched yet. To a glance at the status field, these look identical. A failed flow needs a troubleshooter. A paused flow needs someone to go find the approver.

The execution log resolves this in seconds. Open the record and check the current step and its status. A flow waiting on approval shows that Approval step as current, with a status like Requested or Pending, and no error anywhere — it's simply waiting. A genuinely failed flow shows a specific step with an actual error status and a message explaining what went wrong. Don't infer failure from elapsed time. Infer it from an actual error on an actual step.

Once the log confirms a real failure, two causes show up constantly in production, and both point outside the flow's own logic. An expired or invalid Connection and Credential Alias — the IntegrationHub action fails authentication cleanly, and the fix is refreshing or reassigning that credential, not rewriting the flow. Or the external system the action calls being temporarily unreachable — a connection timeout recorded on that specific step, with nothing wrong in the flow itself.

Both show up as the flow failed, and both get diagnosed the same way: open the step that actually has the error, read what it says, and resist assuming the flow's own configuration is wrong before checking that. Next: a full worked scenario — a stuck integration flow, start to root cause.
